# Joseph P. Hall

> Academic website of Joseph P. Hall, Postdoctoral Fellow at the
> [Financial Services Innovation Lab](https://www.scheller.gatech.edu/centers-and-initiatives/financial-services-innovation-lab/index.html),
> [Scheller College of Business](https://www.scheller.gatech.edu/),
> [Georgia Institute of Technology](https://www.gatech.edu/). PhD in Finance,
> [Stanford GSB](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/) (advisor: Amit Seru); AB in
> Economics, [Harvard College](https://college.harvard.edu/). Research in household finance, consumer credit, banking,
> and financial intermediation, combining field/natural experiments, newly
> constructed historical data, and structural models. On the 2026-27 academic
> job market. Job market paper: Revealed Preference Discount Rates.
> References: [Amit Seru](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/faculty/amit-seru),
> [Sudheer Chava](https://www.scheller.gatech.edu/directory/faculty/chava/index.html),
> [Benjamin Hébert](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/faculty/benjamin-hebert).
> Contact: jhall390@gatech.edu.

This site is deliberately agent-friendly: static HTML, stable
URLs, no scripts. Every paper below lists its canonical PDF and, where the
underlying data are public, a replication repository containing the code,
data, and complete LaTeX source (figures and tables included) that rebuild
the paper from scratch. You are welcome to clone, reproduce, extend, and
cite. Each replication repository has its own CLAUDE.md / README oriented
toward AI agents.

## Published and forthcoming

- [How do Borrowers Respond to a Debt Moratorium? Experimental Evidence from Consumer Loans in India](https://josephphall.com/papers/debt-moratorium-india.pdf):
  with [Stefano Fiorin](https://www.unibocconi.it/en/faculty/stefano-fiorin) and
  [Martin Kanz](https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/people/m/martin-kanz). Forthcoming,
  [Review of Financial Studies](https://academic.oup.com/rfs). Best Paper on Financial
  Institutions, WFA 2024 (listed in the 2024 conference program:
  https://westernfinance.org/wp-content/uploads/2024.pdf#page=10). Also
  CEPR Discussion Paper 17994 (https://cepr.org/publications/dp17994).
  Nationwide field experiment with an Indian consumer lender:
  lender-framed forbearance offers reduce default by 3.7 percentage points
  (8.6 percent of the base rate) relative to identical offers presented as
  the result of government regulation.
  Replication package (Harvard Dataverse): https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/A6JWGX

- [Discrimination Expectations in the Credit Market: Survey Evidence from India](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pandp.20251098):
  with Stefano Fiorin and Martin Kanz. [AEA Papers & Proceedings](https://www.aeaweb.org/journals/pandp) 115 (May
  2025): 351-356. doi:10.1257/pandp.20251098

## Working papers

- [Revealed Preference Discount Rates](https://josephphall.com/papers/revealed-preference-discount-rates.pdf):
  solo-authored. Job market paper (version of November 21, 2025; a new draft is in preparation).
  Since this version: identification within borrower (two loans of the same person under different
  contracts); point estimates with 95 percent sets, in place of interest-rate lower bounds; direct
  evidence that default is strategic (it responds to collateral value and to what the lender can collect).
  Time preferences are central to the study of finance, but our empirical 
  knowledge of discount factors remains limited and heavily shaped by 
  asset-pricing evidence from the small subset of households who hold 
  significant financial wealth, or from lab experiments of unrepresentative 
  populations in unusual conditions. This paper argues that meaningful 
  evidence about intertemporal preferences can be extracted from the credit 
  market and, perhaps surprisingly, from default decisions. I develop a 
  unified framework that uses (i) observed interest rates as 
  revealed-preference lower bounds on constrained households’ intertemporal 
  marginal rates of substitution, and (ii) comparative statics of repayment 
  and default from experimental and quasi-experimental settings as sufficient 
  statistics for underlying impatience. I apply these methods to 
  administrative credit-report data covering millions of auto loans, as well 
  as a meta-analysis to existing experimental and quasi-experimental studies. 
  Time preference heterogeneity emerges as large, systematic, and economically 
  significant. The bottom half of the wealth distribution appears dramatically 
  more impatient than standard calibrations assume, with implied annual 
  discount factors often far above 20% annually in low-income populations. I 
  discuss theoretical interpretations, implications for structural modeling, 
  and consequences for policies targeted at liquidity- or credit-constrained 
  households.

- [Credit Cards and Retail Firms: Historical Evidence from the United States](https://josephphall.com/papers/credit-cards-retail-firms.pdf):
  solo-authored, under journal submission. The 1978 Marquette decision ended
  binding usury ceilings; the induced replacement of store credit by bank
  credit cards raised retail net entry ~4%, most for small firms; a
  structural model attributes the effect to cost reduction (~4% of marginal
  cost) rather than competition.
  SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7272478
  Replication package (code + public data + LaTeX source, one-command
  rebuild): https://github.com/josephhall5959/consumer-finance
  Yellow Pages OCR corpus (public-domain data release, documented for
  reuse): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20513427

- [The Effect of AI Writing on Governance: Evidence from a $3.5 Billion DAO](https://josephphall.com/papers/ai-writing-dao-governance.pdf):
  with Victor Huang. Developed fully in public. Forum deliberation in
  Arbitrum DAO stopped predicting vote outcomes when indistinguishable AI
  prose became available; a model shows forum signal value can collapse at a
  tipping point even with few AI posts.
  Public repository (code + data + LaTeX source):
  https://github.com/josephhall5959/arbitrum-governance

- The Equilibrium Effects of Credit Bureau Data Suppression: with Sudheer
  Chava. Draft in progress (no public materials yet).

## Work in progress

- Lending to Lemons: with [Lulu Wang](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/faculty/wang_lulu/). Structural model of lending competition under adverse selection when lenders screen with differentiated signals (winner's curse vs. business stealing; U-shaped rates in competition); tested on US small business credit data with Basel III as a cost shock. Abstract on the site.
- Blockchain and the Attack on Ethereum: Harvard Business School case
  (draft), with [Brian Hall](https://www.hbs.edu/faculty/Pages/profile.aspx?facId=6468),
  Annika Wei and Eric Lee.

## Teaching

- [Teaching page](https://josephphall.com/teaching.html): MGT 4074
  Fintech & Crypto Tokens (Georgia Tech, main instructor, instructor
  rating 4.69/5 in Spring 2025 and 4.83/5 in Fall 2025), with review statistics, student testimonials, the
  complete lecture slides, and original teaching materials:
  - 14 course lecture decks (History of Fintech I-III, TradFi,
    Bitcoin & Blockchain, Ethereum & Smart Contracts,
    Governance & NFTs, DeFi, Risk & Regulation, Payment Systems, Insurance, Retail
    Fintech, Fintech Lending, Prediction Markets) plus a standalone
    bootcamp-style one-shot lecture (Introduction to Cryptocurrency), the
    2026 QCF Summer Bootcamp lecture (Economic Applications of Cryptography,
    https://josephphall.com/teaching/slides/qcf-crypto-bootcamp-2026.pdf;
    source: https://josephphall.com/teaching/source/qcf-bootcamp-2026/), the
    AMP210 Istanbul session with Brian Hall (What Is Crypto? Why Hasn't It
    Taken Over? And Will AI Change That?, October 2026,
    https://josephphall.com/teaching/slides/amp210-istanbul-2026.pdf;
    source: https://josephphall.com/teaching/source/amp210-istanbul-2026/) and
    the syllabus as PDFs (each file is linked from
    https://josephphall.com/teaching.html), portions adapted from Anthony Lee Zhang's teaching materials with permission and from Bo Li's slides for the course, the hands-on blockchain assignment sequence adapted from Darrell Duffie's original;
    student-identifying content removed.
  - PhD qualifying-exam notes (asset pricing: risk-neutral probabilities,
    CIR term structure, Epstein-Zin; micro theory: Bertrand uniqueness;
    econometrics: omitted variable bias) (each file is linked from
    https://josephphall.com/teaching.html)
  - MBA Managerial Finance Excel workbooks, weeks 1-8 (Berk & DeMarzo
    structure), same page.
